newsitem.title: USA: U.S. congressman to visit N.Korea in Hunziker case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. congressman to visit N.Korea in Hunziker case.

text.p: A U.S. congressman who often acts as an unofficial envoy of the Clinton administration will visit North Korea shortly amid signs Pyongyang may be about to release an American detained there for three months.
New Mexico Democrat Bill Richardson will travel to the isolated Stalinist state early next week, his spokesman said on Thursday.
"The only thing we're commenting on is that he is hoping he can secure the release of this young American, Mr (Carl) Hunziker," the spokesman, Stu Nagurka, said.
"There's no guarantee that he'll secure his release, but he's going to make an effort to do so."

Hunziker, 26, was arrested on Aug. 24 after crossing the Yalu River from China into North Korea and was accused of espionage. Hunziker, whose father lives in Washington state, denied the charges and said he was a missionary.

The State Department, which did not disclose the incident for several weeks, ridiculed the spying charges and demanded Hunziker's release. Earlier this month, in an apparent change of tone, Pyongyang began to call it a "humanitarian" case.

State Department spokesman Glyn Davies said the administration fully supported the trip by Richardson, who has gone on several previous missions to countries with which Washington has poor or no relations, including North Korea.
"We view it as an important humanitarian mission," Davies told a news briefing.

U.S. officials said Richardson would be accompanied by an official of the State Department's East Asia bureau, Eric John. They described John as an "escort officer" and said he would not be engaging in negotiations with North Korea.
The officials said they placed high hopes on Richardson's trip, and one said: "We have reason to believe his mission will be successful."
He declined to elaborate, but U.S. and North Korean officials have held a series of meetings on the Hunziker case at the United Nations in New York.

Richardson had planned to visit North Korea in September but called off the trip after an intrusion by a North Korean submarine into South Korean waters sparked a major crisis between the two countries.
